extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and educated readers interested in late-19th-century astronomy and physical chemistry
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and inferential criteria for assessing the nebular hypothesis and related cosmogonic/chemical propositions, using observational, experimental, and theoretical grounds drawn from chemistry, spectrum analysis, and dynamical astronomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special evidences for elements being compound
rubrics_metrics.description: Special reasons: the parallelism between allotropy and isomerism; the numerous lines in the spectrum of each element; and the cyclical law of Newlands and Mendeljeff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented in Note I as 'special' chemical/chemico-physical lines of evidence that support the belief that the so-called elements are compounds; these are to be weighed alongside more general (cosmical) reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori inference from the general law of evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The general law of evolution affords an a priori ground for suspecting that the so-called elements are compounds, because matter progressed from relative homogeneity to heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the broad, cosmical principle of progressive increase in heterogeneity as a legitimate inferential tool when interpreting chemical constitution in early solar-system material; treat it as supportive even without direct induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive evidence from increasing crust heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the cooling of the Earth, the components of its crust have been ever increasing in heterogeneity; chemical evolution has proceeded from simple to increasingly complex substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe temporal sequences (oxides → salts → organic bodies) and use the trend toward greater variety and complexity in known chemical history as inductive support for earlier homogeneity and thus for compound nature of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affinity and stability trends across chemical complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: As we move from modern complex nitrogenous bodies to oxy-hydro-carbons to inorganic salts to simple oxides/acids, affinities and stabilities generally increase; complex modern molecules show smaller affinities and stabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the pattern of chemical affinities and molecular stability (higher affinity/stability for simpler types) as suggesting that 'simple' undecomposable substances could themselves be compounds formed under far stronger affinities in earlier conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of molecular-weight trends between compounds and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast of ascending molecular weights in known compounds with those of the so-called elements shows analogous appearance of certain characters (e.g., high-molecular-weight bodies being chemically inert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarity of trends (e.g., increasing molecular weight associated with certain inertness) to argue by analogy that elements might be composite, mirroring compound classes' properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat evolution decreases with increasing molecular complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat evolved during formation of simple compounds is greater than that evolved during formation of complex compounds; among elements, unions of low molecular weights give more heat than unions of high molecular weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Andrews' and other experimental observations about heat of formation to infer that proto-chemical combinations forming elements would have released very large heats, affecting nebular thermal history and chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proto-chemical combinations as necessary enablers of condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Only through instrumentality of combinations which formed the elements did the concentration of diffused nebulous matter into concrete masses become possible; simpler units had to combine to reduce resistance to liquefaction/density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling nebular condensation, include proto-chemical combination as a heat-generating and condensation-enabling process; recognize that such reactions could dominate heat balance in early stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for two heat sources during nebular condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish heat due to proto-chemical combinations from heat due to contraction by gravitation (both interpretable as loss of motion); their relative shares vary between early (combination-dominated) and late (gravitation-dominated) stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thermal evolution models must partition heat contributions between chemical combination and gravitational contraction and consider how that affects timing and final states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of solar-heat-duration estimates on initial temperature and proto-chemical history
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates of past period of high solar emission and future duration of solar heat must depend on assumed initial temperatures and whether proto-chemical changes (with large associated heats) are taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic gravitational-contraction-only estimates of solar lifetime; incorporate possible additional heat reservoirs/releases from element-forming reactions which can lengthen/delay emission timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of critical temperature (Andrews) for liquefaction arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: For each kind of gaseous matter a temperature exists above which no amount of pressure will cause liquefaction; if internal mass is above critical temperature, gases remain unliquified however great the pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concept of critical temperature to infer where and when liquefaction will commence in a condensing spheroid (centre-first vs periphery-first) and hence infer internal planetary structure outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size-dependent sequence of liquefaction and solidification
rubrics_metrics.description: In small spheroids liquefaction/solidification may begin at the centre and spread outward; in much larger spheroids the critical temperature is reached first in outer parts, producing liquefaction in strata between centre and surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predict internal structures (molten shell with gaseous nucleus vs central molten region) based on spheroid mass/size, convection, and where critical conditions for phase change are first met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms supporting crust formation on molten shells
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid crust may form on a molten shell because (1) some metals expand on solidifying and float, and (2) accumulation of lower-density compounds (oxides, chlorides, sulphurets) on the molten shell will be supported by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating crust formation, consider both material-specific volume changes on solidification and compositional layering from accumulated low-density compounds as supporting mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planetary instability via proto-chemical reactions as source of fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A planet with a gaseous nucleus is liable to catastrophe: if components of the nucleus suddenly enter into proto-chemical combinations forming a new element, an explosion could shatter the planet and eject fragments (planetoids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing catastrophic origins for minor planets, examine whether internal proto-chemical change could provide the energetic mechanism and whether size/conditions (e.g., a body between Jupiter and Mars) make it plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planetoid discovery rate and magnitude distribution as empirical constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate of discovery and average magnitudes of newly discovered planetoids (comparison of 1868 versus 1888 data) inform whether the number of planetoids is limited or effectively unlimited; continued discoveries of similar magnitudes suggest many more exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical evidence (discovery rates, average magnitudes over time) to assess hypotheses about total population sizes; apparent constancy or growth argues against a small finite population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbital eccentricity and inclination diversity tests ring-origin hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide range and miscellany of mean distances, eccentricities, and inclinations among planetoids (far exceeding neighbouring planets') are difficult to reconcile with origin from a single nebulous ring with uniform properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ring-fragmentation models by checking whether they can plausibly produce the observed large spreads and jumbled distribution of orbital elements; if not, consider alternative formation scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angular velocity uniformity requirement for ring-to-planetoid models
rubrics_metrics.description: The tacit assumption that parts of a nebulous ring have the same angular velocities is unlikely to hold if derived orbital periods vary greatly (e.g., Thule vs Medusa), implying inner ring portions would need much higher angular velocity than outer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test ring-origin hypotheses against required angular-velocity distributions implied by observed orbital periods; large discrepancies indicate the ring model may be implausible without additional mechanisms.
